card.before: Equilibrium constants follow the algebra of reaction equations. Reversing a reaction takes the reciprocal of its constant; multiplying its coefficients raises the constant to that power. Adding reactions multiplies their constants, letting a difficult equilibrium be assembled from known ones.
card.after: At a common temperature, equilibrium constants follow the algebra of reaction equations. Reversing a reaction takes the reciprocal of its constant; multiplying coefficients raises the constant to that power. Adding reactions multiplies their constants, letting a difficult equilibrium be assembled from known ones.

card.before: Le Châtelier’s principle predicts how an equilibrium responds when conditions change. Compressing a gaseous mixture favors the side with fewer gas molecules when the two sides differ. Temperature changes can also shift equilibrium, with the direction depending on whether heat is absorbed or released.
card.after: Le Châtelier’s principle predicts how equilibrium responds when conditions change. At fixed temperature, compressing a gaseous mixture favors the side with fewer gas molecules when the sides differ. Temperature changes also shift equilibrium, with direction depending on whether the reaction absorbs or releases heat.

card.before: For a first-order reaction, each successive half-life removes half of the reactant still present. The half-life depends on the rate constant, not the starting concentration. Equal time intervals therefore produce equal fractional losses rather than equal amounts of material disappearing.
card.after: Under fixed conditions, each successive half-life of a first-order reaction removes half the reactant still present. The half-life depends on the rate constant, not the starting concentration. Equal time intervals therefore produce equal fractional losses rather than equal amounts disappearing.

card.before: Activation energy is the energy barrier reactants must overcome to reach a transition state along a reaction pathway. Collisions can fail even when molecules meet: insufficient energy prevents productive rearrangement. A higher barrier leaves fewer collisions energetic enough to react at a given temperature.
card.after: In a collision model, activation energy marks the barrier reactants must overcome to reach a transition state. Collisions can fail even when molecules meet: insufficient energy prevents productive rearrangement. A higher barrier leaves fewer collisions energetic enough to react at a given temperature.

card.before: A crystal structure is a repeating pattern of atoms. Its ordered arrangement extends through space rather than ending at the edge of a drawn box. Describing the repeating cell and the atomic positions separates the geometry of repetition from the substance occupying it.
card.after: A periodic crystal structure is a repeating pattern of atoms. Its ordered arrangement extends through space rather than ending at the edge of a drawn box. Describing the repeating cell and atomic positions separates the geometry of repetition from the substance occupying it.

card.before: A covalent network solid contains atoms joined in an extended web of covalent bonds. Melting or breaking that network requires disrupting those bonds, rather than merely separating intact molecules. Diamond exemplifies the resulting combination of hardness and a very high melting temperature.
card.after: A covalent network solid contains atoms joined in an extended web of covalent bonds. Disrupting that network requires breaking bonds, rather than merely separating intact molecules. Such solids often have high melting temperatures; diamond illustrates the hardness that extensive covalent bonding can produce.

card.before: A body-centered cubic crystal has atoms at a cube’s corners and one at its center. Sharing the corner atoms with neighboring cells gives two atoms per conventional cell. Each atom has eight nearest neighbors, illustrating how an apparently simple arrangement determines local coordination.
card.after: A monatomic body-centered cubic crystal has atoms at a cube’s corners and one at its center. Sharing corner atoms with neighboring cells gives two atoms per conventional cell. Each atom has eight nearest neighbors, illustrating how the arrangement determines local coordination.

card.before: A face-centered cubic structure places atoms at cube corners and face centers. Shared boundaries leave four atoms per conventional cell, with twelve nearest neighbors around each atom. The same arrangement can be described as cubic close packing, using an ABC sequence of layers.
card.after: A monatomic face-centered cubic structure places atoms at cube corners and face centers. Shared boundaries leave four atoms per conventional cell, with twelve nearest neighbors around each atom. The arrangement can also be described as cubic close packing, using an ABC layer sequence.

card.before: Hexagonal close packing builds a solid from alternating AB layers. The third layer sits above the first, unlike the ABC sequence of cubic close packing. Both arrangements give each atom twelve nearest neighbors, so equal coordination does not imply identical layer geometry.
card.after: Ideal hexagonal close packing builds a solid from alternating AB layers. The third layer sits above the first, unlike the ABC sequence of cubic close packing. Both arrangements give each atom twelve nearest neighbors, so equal coordination does not imply identical layer geometry.

before.locator: 10.4 Phase Diagrams; inspected passage indices 12, 25 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm105744432; fs-idm71881152
before.note: Three phases coexist at one pressure-temperature combination on a pure-substance phase diagram.

after.locator: 10.4 Phase Diagrams; inspected passage indices 12, 25, 40 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm105744432; fs-idm71881152; fs-idm114606944
after.note: The water and carbon-dioxide phase diagrams show three-phase coexistence and distinguish it from disappearance of the liquid–vapor boundary at the critical point.

before.note: The phase-diagram passage explicitly describes the triple point as three phases coexisting in equilibrium.

after.note: The phase diagrams contrast a triple point, where three phases coexist, with a critical point, where the liquid–vapor distinction ends; this is a comparative learning bridge, not a hierarchy.

card.before: The method of initial rates compares reaction speeds measured soon after mixing different starting concentrations. Holding one concentration fixed while changing another helps isolate its influence. Ratios of the measured rates reveal reaction orders before the resulting rate law is used to find the constant.
card.after: The method of initial rates compares reaction speeds measured soon after mixing different starting concentrations under otherwise matched conditions. Holding one concentration fixed while changing another isolates its influence. Rate ratios reveal reaction orders before the resulting rate law is used to find the constant.

card.before: A titration indicator works best when its color change falls within the steep part of the pH curve near equivalence. In a weak-acid/strong-base titration, phenolphthalein can work well while methyl orange changes too early, giving a misleading stopping signal.
card.after: Choosing a titration indicator means matching its color-change interval to the steep part of the pH curve near equivalence. An indicator that changes earlier can give a premature stopping signal; one suitable for a strong acid may fail for a weak acid.

before.locator: 14.6 Buffers; inspected passage indices 7, 8 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm127493136; fs-idp41915456
before.note: A weak conjugate acid-base pair consumes small additions of strong acid or base.

after.locator: 14.6 Buffers; inspected passage indices 7, 8, 38 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-idm127493136; fs-idp41915456; fs-idm103629216
after.note: A weak conjugate pair consumes modest additions of strong acid or base; the finite component amounts determine buffer capacity.

card.before: Two buffers can have the same pH yet tolerate very different additions of acid or base. Buffer capacity depends on how much of the conjugate pair is present. Increasing both components together can raise that capacity without changing their ratio and initial pH.
card.after: Buffers with nearly the same pH can tolerate very different additions of acid or base. Buffer capacity depends on how much of the conjugate pair is present. Increasing both components together can raise capacity while approximately preserving their ratio-dependent initial pH.

card.before: Electroplating deposits a metal coating onto a conducting object by reducing dissolved metal ions at its surface. In silver plating, the object serves as the cathode while a silver anode supplies metal. Current, voltage, and solution composition influence the resulting coating’s quality.
card.after: Electroplating deposits metal onto a conducting object by reducing dissolved metal ions at its surface. In one silver-plating setup, the object serves as cathode while a silver anode supplies metal. Current, voltage, and solution composition influence the coating’s quality.

card.before: Zone refining purifies silicon by moving a narrow molten region along a solid rod. Impurities preferentially enter the liquid and travel with that moving zone. They collect toward one end, which is removed, leaving material suitable for demanding semiconductor applications.
card.after: Zone refining purifies silicon by moving a narrow molten region along a solid rod. Impurities more soluble in the melt travel with that moving zone. Removing an impurity-rich end improves the material’s purity, supporting the preparation of silicon for semiconductor manufacture.

card.before: Silicon can protect itself with a thin surface layer of silicon dioxide. This passivation changes how the underlying material reacts with its surroundings. When a strong base removes the oxide, the exposed silicon can react, illustrating how surface chemistry can dominate a bulk material’s behavior.
card.after: Silicon can protect itself with a thin surface layer of silicon dioxide. This passivation changes how the underlying material reacts with its surroundings. When hot, strong aqueous base removes the oxide, exposed silicon can react, illustrating the importance of surface chemistry to bulk behavior.

card.before: Topology studies properties of spaces that survive continuous changes of shape. Stretching a circle into an ellipse changes lengths but preserves its connected loop. Focusing on such structure lets mathematicians compare objects without treating every geometric distortion as a fundamentally new space.
card.after: Topology studies properties of spaces preserved by continuous, reversible changes of shape. Stretching a circle into an ellipse changes lengths but preserves its connected loop. Focusing on such structure lets mathematicians compare objects without treating every geometric distortion as a fundamentally new space.

card.before: The Euler characteristic packages a space’s structure into a number. For a triangulated closed surface, vertices minus edges plus faces gives this invariant. A sphere and a torus have different values, revealing a distinction that persists when either surface is smoothly reshaped.
card.after: The Euler characteristic packages a space’s structure into a number. For a finite triangulation of a closed surface, vertices minus edges plus faces gives this invariant. A sphere and a torus have different values, revealing a distinction that persists when either surface is smoothly reshaped.

card.before: A geodesic is a locally length-minimizing path determined by a space’s geometry. In a plane it is straight; on a sphere it follows a great circle. Local shortestness matters: continuing along a great circle far enough need not give the shortest route between its endpoints.
card.after: In Riemannian geometry, a geodesic is a locally length-minimizing path. In a plane it is straight; on a sphere it follows a great circle. Local shortestness matters: continuing along a great circle far enough need not give the shortest route between its endpoints.

card.before: Gaussian curvature is the product of the two principal curvatures at a surface point. Matching curvature signs give a positive product; opposite signs give a negative one. This is an intrinsic geometric quantity, independent of the coordinates chosen to describe the surface.
card.after: Gaussian curvature is the product of the two principal curvatures at a surface point. Matching nonzero signs give a positive product; opposite signs give a negative one. This is an intrinsic geometric quantity, independent of the coordinates chosen to describe the surface.

card.before: For a compact two-dimensional surface without boundary, the Gauss–Bonnet theorem links total Gaussian curvature to its Euler characteristic: the curvature integral equals two pi times that number. Smoothly changing the shape can redistribute curvature while leaving this topologically determined total unchanged.
card.after: For a compact smooth two-dimensional surface without boundary, the Gauss–Bonnet theorem links total Gaussian curvature to its Euler characteristic: the curvature integral equals two pi times that number. Changing the shape can redistribute curvature while leaving this topologically determined total unchanged.

card.before: A spanning tree keeps every vertex of a connected graph while using just enough edges to preserve connectivity without cycles. For n vertices it has n minus one edges. Different choices can connect the same graph, so a network may have many spanning trees.
card.after: A spanning tree keeps every vertex of a finite connected graph while using just enough edges to preserve connectivity without cycles. For n vertices it has n minus one edges. Different choices can connect the same graph, so a network may have many spanning trees.

card.before: The matrix-tree theorem turns a counting problem into a determinant. Form a graph’s Laplacian from vertex degrees and adjacency, then remove the same row and column. For a simple, unweighted, undirected graph, the resulting determinant counts its spanning trees, avoiding an explicit listing of every tree.
card.after: The matrix-tree theorem turns counting into a determinant. Form a graph’s Laplacian from vertex degrees and adjacency, then remove the same row and column. For a finite, simple, unweighted, undirected graph, the resulting determinant counts spanning trees, avoiding an explicit listing of every tree.

card.before: A graph’s chromatic polynomial counts its proper vertex colorings for any specified number of available colors. Adjacent vertices must receive different colors, and color names are distinguishable. Evaluating the polynomial answers a whole family of counting questions rather than only finding the fewest necessary colors.
card.after: A finite undirected graph’s chromatic polynomial counts its proper vertex colorings for any specified number of available colors. Adjacent vertices must receive different colors, and color names are distinguishable. Evaluating the polynomial answers many counting questions rather than only finding the fewest necessary colors.

card.before: A Ramsey number measures how large a graph must become before a specified pattern is unavoidable. Every sufficiently large graph contains either a clique of one chosen size or an independent set of another. The familiar party version translates edges into pairs of people who know each other.
card.after: A Ramsey number gives the smallest vertex count that forces either a clique of one chosen size or an independent set of another in any simple undirected graph. The party analogy treats vertices as people and edges as mutual acquaintance.

card.before: Catalan numbers appear when counting ways to triangulate a regular polygon without crossing diagonals. The same sequence also arises in tree-enumeration problems. Such repeated appearances suggest a useful strategy: translate one counting problem into another structure whose possibilities are already understood.
card.after: Catalan numbers appear when counting ways to triangulate a regular polygon with fixed vertices using noncrossing diagonals. The same sequence arises in tree-enumeration problems. Such repeated appearances suggest a useful strategy: translate one counting problem into another structure whose possibilities are already understood.

before.note: The quotient-group source connects the sizes of groups and cosets with Lagrange’s group theorem.

after.note: For finite groups, the quotient-group source connects the sizes of groups and cosets with Lagrange’s group theorem; the quotient construction itself need not be finite.

card.before: The exponential distribution models waiting times between events in a constant-rate Poisson process. Its probability density decreases as the waiting time grows. It is memoryless: having already waited does not change the distribution of the additional time until the next event.
card.after: The exponential distribution models waiting times between events in a positive constant-rate Poisson process. Its probability density decreases as the waiting time grows. It is memoryless: having already waited does not change the distribution of the additional time until the next event.

card.before: The geometric distribution describes how long repeated independent trials with a fixed success probability take to produce a first success. Some conventions count preceding failures from zero; others count trials from one. Keeping that convention explicit prevents an otherwise correct formula from being shifted by one.
card.after: The geometric distribution describes how long repeated independent trials with a fixed positive success probability take to produce a first success. Some conventions count preceding failures from zero; others count trials from one. Keeping that convention explicit prevents an otherwise correct formula from being shifted by one.

card.before: Conditional expectation averages a random quantity while retaining specified information, such as the value of another variable. The result can itself vary with that information rather than being one fixed number. Its mathematical definition preserves the appropriate averages over events recognizable from the conditioning information.
card.after: Conditional expectation averages an integrable random quantity while retaining specified information, such as another variable’s value. The result can itself vary with that information rather than being one fixed number. Its mathematical definition preserves the appropriate averages over events recognizable from the conditioning information.

card.before: A martingale is a random process whose expected next value, given its recorded history, equals its current value. It may still fluctuate substantially. A symmetric one-dimensional random walk illustrates the idea: either step is possible, but their conditional average produces no expected change.
card.after: A martingale is a random process with finite expectations whose expected next value, given its history, equals its current value. It can still fluctuate substantially. A symmetric one-dimensional random walk illustrates this: either step is possible, but their conditional average produces no expected change.

card.before: Markov’s inequality bounds the chance that a nonnegative random quantity exceeds a positive threshold using only its mean. Divide the mean by the threshold to obtain the bound. No specific distribution shape is required, but dropping the nonnegativity condition would invalidate this argument.
card.after: Markov’s inequality bounds the chance that a nonnegative random quantity exceeds a positive threshold using only its finite mean. Divide the mean by the threshold to obtain the bound. No specific distribution shape is required, but dropping nonnegativity would invalidate this argument.

card.before: A constant-rate Poisson process models events with independent counts in nonoverlapping time intervals. Over a sufficiently short interval, one event has probability proportional to its length, while multiple events become negligible. Random clustering remains possible even though the model’s average rate stays constant.
card.after: A constant-rate Poisson process has independent event counts in nonoverlapping time intervals. For very short intervals, one-event probability is approximately proportional to duration, while multiple events become negligible by comparison. Random clusters can occur even though the model’s average event rate stays constant.

card.before: In the classic gambler’s ruin model, two players repeatedly transfer one unit according to a fair coin until one has everything. With finite starting funds, absorption eventually occurs with probability one. The player starting with less has a greater probability of losing everything despite the fair odds.
card.after: In the gambler’s ruin model, two players transfer one unit after each independent fair coin toss until one has everything. With finite starting funds, absorption eventually occurs with probability one. The player starting with less has a greater chance of losing everything despite fair odds.

card.before: Energy can change form or move between a system and its surroundings without being created or destroyed. Mechanical energy is a narrower account: it can change when nonconservative forces do work. Choosing the system and included energy forms prevents an apparent loss from being misread.
card.after: In a mechanical system, energy can change form or cross its boundary without being created or destroyed. Mechanical energy alone can decrease when nonconservative forces act. Choosing the system and included energy forms prevents energy transferred into heat from looking like unexplained loss.

before.locator: 8.3 Conservation of Energy; inspected passage indices 6, 10, 11, 13 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1165036730634; fs-id1165037156176; fs-id1165037052216; fs-id1165036788158
before.note: Track energy transfers and transformations without confusing total energy with mechanical energy alone.

after.locator: 8.3 Conservation of Energy; inspected passage indices 6, 10, 11, 13 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1165036730634; fs-id1165037156176; fs-id1165037052216; fs-id1165036788158
after.note: Classical energy accounting distinguishes total energy transfer from changes in mechanical energy.

after.locator: 15.5 Damped Oscillations; inspected passage indices 9 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167131181569
after.note: The damped oscillator loses mechanical energy, usually transferred into thermal energy.

card.before: Buoyancy comes from a fluid’s pressure increasing with depth, giving an immersed object a net upward force. That force equals the weight of displaced fluid. It still acts on an object that sinks; sinking simply means the object’s downward weight is larger.
card.after: In a static fluid under gravity, pressure increases with depth, producing buoyancy equal to the weight of displaced fluid. Buoyancy still acts on an object released from rest to sink: its weight exceeds that upward force, so it initially accelerates downward.

card.before: Angular momentum combines a particle’s linear momentum with its position relative to a chosen origin. Even straight-line motion can have angular momentum about a point away from that path. Choosing a different origin changes the lever arm, so this rotational quantity is not defined by speed alone.
card.after: For a classical particle, angular momentum combines linear momentum with position relative to a chosen origin. Even straight-line motion can have angular momentum about a point away from that path. A different origin changes the lever arm, so this quantity is not defined by speed alone.

card.before: Gravitational potential energy changes as attracting masses move closer together or farther apart. Choosing zero energy at infinite separation makes the energy negative for a finite separation. Over large distances, gravity varies, so a constant-gravity height formula is only a local approximation.
card.after: For two separated masses in Newtonian gravity, choosing zero gravitational potential energy at infinite separation makes it negative at finite separation. Bringing the masses closer lowers it. A constant-gravity height formula is only a local approximation when the gravitational field changes little.

before.locator: 15.6 Forced Oscillations; inspected passage indices 16 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167131421041
before.note: Lower damping produces a narrower resonant response and more selective frequency discrimination.

after.locator: 15.6 Forced Oscillations; inspected passage indices 16 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167131421041
after.note: Light damping produces narrow resonance curves and high frequency selectivity; the tuned-radio example applies this qualitative relation.

after.locator: 15.5 Damped Oscillations; inspected passage indices 9 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1167131181569
after.note: Weak damping lets oscillations persist while their amplitude gradually decreases.

before.note: The source introduces quality factor through the width and damping of resonant oscillator responses.

after.note: The source introduces quality factor through the width and damping of resonant oscillator responses.

card.before: Tidal locking synchronizes a body’s rotation with its orbital motion through long-term tidal interactions and dissipation. Earth’s Moon therefore keeps the same face toward Earth while still rotating. The familiar fixed-looking lunar face is evidence of matched rotation and orbital periods, not absence of spin.
card.after: Tidal locking synchronizes a body’s rotation with its orbital motion through long-term tidal interactions and dissipation. Earth’s Moon therefore keeps roughly the same face toward Earth while still rotating. The fixed-looking lunar face reflects matched rotation and orbital periods, not absence of spin.

card.before: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels toward a lower-index medium at an incidence angle beyond the critical angle. Instead of a propagating refracted ray emerging, light is reflected back. The index ordering is essential: increasing the angle at any arbitrary boundary is not sufficient.
card.after: At an ideal nonabsorbing interface, total internal reflection occurs toward a lower-index medium at an incidence angle beyond the critical angle. Instead of a propagating refracted ray emerging, light is reflected back. The index ordering matters: increasing the angle at an arbitrary boundary is insufficient.

card.before: The Rayleigh criterion gives a conventional diffraction-based test for resolving two point sources. With an ideal circular aperture, they are just resolved when one pattern’s central maximum falls on the other’s first minimum. Larger apertures or shorter wavelengths permit smaller angular separations by this criterion.
card.after: The Rayleigh criterion conventionally treats two point sources as just resolved when one diffraction maximum meets the other’s first minimum. For an ideal circular aperture much wider than the wavelength, increasing aperture size or shortening wavelength reduces the corresponding angular separation.

card.before: In the photoelectric effect, sufficiently high-frequency light ejects electrons from a material. A stopping voltage measures the largest kinetic energy of those electrons. Brighter illumination can increase the photocurrent without changing that stopping voltage, showing why an individual electron’s energy is not determined by brightness alone.
card.after: In ordinary single-photon photoemission, light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons from a metal. The stopping voltage measures their maximum kinetic energy. At fixed frequency, brighter illumination can increase photocurrent without increasing that maximum energy, separating electron number from energy per electron.

before.locator: 6.2 Photoelectric Effect; inspected passage indices 6, 14, 15, 20 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1163709773708; fs-id1163713174554; fs-id1163713274860; fs-id1163713428401
before.note: Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons whose maximum energy is measured with a stopping potential.

after.locator: 6.2 Photoelectric Effect; inspected passage indices 6, 14, 15, 20, 21, 22, 23, 25 (zero-based in saved snapshot); HTML anchors: fs-id1163709773708; fs-id1163713174554; fs-id1163713274860; fs-id1163713428401; fs-id1163709678905; fs-id1163713527138; fs-id1163713118837; fs-id1163713536791
after.note: The monochromatic, individual-photon model links threshold and maximum electron energy to photon frequency; varying intensity at fixed frequency changes current rather than stopping voltage.

card.before: A scanning tunneling microscope brings a sharp conducting tip extremely close to a biased sample. Electrons tunnel across the gap, and the current changes strongly with tip–surface separation. Monitoring that current while scanning reveals atomic-scale structure through electronic behavior rather than ordinary reflected-light imaging.
card.after: A scanning tunneling microscope brings a sharp conducting tip extremely close to a biased conducting sample. Electrons tunnel across the gap, and current changes strongly with tip–surface separation. Monitoring that current while scanning reveals atomic-scale structure through electronic behavior rather than ordinary reflected-light imaging.

card.before: The Stern–Gerlach experiment sent silver atoms through a nonuniform magnetic field and produced two separated bands. A classical picture allowing every magnetic orientation would instead predict a continuous spread. The result reveals quantized angular-momentum projections associated with the atoms’ unpaired electron spin.
card.after: The Stern–Gerlach experiment sent ground-state silver atoms through a nonuniform magnetic field and produced two separated bands. A classical picture allowing every magnetic orientation would predict a continuous spread. The result reveals quantized angular-momentum projections associated with the atoms’ unpaired electron spin.

card.before: The James Webb Space Telescope uses a five-layer sunshield to limit infrared radiation arriving from the Sun, Earth, and Moon. This thermal protection supports observations of faint cosmic targets. Webb operates around the Sun near the second Sun–Earth Lagrange point, rather than circling close to Earth.
card.after: The James Webb Space Telescope uses a five-layer sunshield to limit infrared radiation arriving from the Sun, Earth, and Moon. It observes early cosmic history from an orbit around the Sun near the second Sun–Earth Lagrange point, rather than circling close to Earth.

card.before: Herschel studied the cool Universe in far-infrared and submillimeter light. Its cameras and high-resolution spectrometer were cooled close to absolute zero. These instruments let astronomers examine forming stars and galaxies and trace water and other material involved in planetary systems.
card.after: Herschel studied the cool Universe in far-infrared and submillimeter light. Detectors in its cameras and high-resolution spectrometer were cooled close to absolute zero. These instruments let astronomers examine forming stars and galaxies and trace water and other material involved in planetary systems.

card.before: Spitzer’s original cryogenic design cooled its telescope assembly to about five kelvin using liquid helium. Suppressing the observatory’s own infrared emission helped it study relatively cool cosmic objects. The case shows why an infrared telescope’s thermal environment can matter as much as its ability to collect light.
card.after: Spitzer’s original cryogenic design cooled its telescope assembly to about five kelvin using liquid helium. Suppressing the observatory’s own infrared emission helped prevent its thermal glow from interfering with observations of relatively cold cosmic objects.

card.before: TESS was designed to search bright stars across the sky for periodic dimming caused by planetary transits. Bright host stars make promising candidates easier to examine with other telescopes. Its survey strategy therefore connects planet detection with later measurements of planetary masses, compositions, and atmospheres.
card.after: TESS was designed to search bright stars across the sky for periodic dimming caused by planetary transits. Bright host stars make promising candidates easier to examine with other telescopes. Its survey strategy connects planet detection with follow-up studies of planetary masses, compositions, and atmospheres.

card.before: NuSTAR observes high-energy X-rays from regions around black holes, exploding stars, and active galaxies. Its measurements have helped determine black-hole spin, connecting radiation from extreme environments with otherwise inaccessible physical properties. The mission illustrates how choosing an observing energy band shapes the questions a telescope can answer.
card.after: NuSTAR uses high-energy X-rays to study regions around black holes, exploding stars, and active galaxies. Its observations have helped estimate black-hole spin, illustrating how radiation from an object’s surroundings can carry information about the object itself.

card.before: Proper motion is a star’s angular change of position across the sky over time. It differs from motion toward or away from us measured by radial velocity. Combining proper motion, distance, and radial velocity lets astronomers reconstruct the star’s actual movement through space.
card.after: Proper motion is a star’s persistent angular drift across the sky over time. It differs from motion toward or away from us measured by radial velocity. Combining proper motion, distance, and radial velocity lets astronomers reconstruct the star’s actual movement through space.

card.before: Material fatigue accumulates damage under repeated loading, sometimes at stresses below the ordinary yield point. Local flaws can concentrate deformation and develop into cracks that grow over many cycles. A load that appears harmless once can therefore become dangerous when repeatedly applied to the same component.
card.after: Material fatigue accumulates damage under repeated loading, sometimes below the ordinary yield point. In metals, local flaws can concentrate deformation and develop into cracks that grow over many cycles. A load that appears harmless once can therefore become dangerous when repeatedly applied to the same component.

card.before: A truss member can carry zero axial force under one particular loading pattern. At an unloaded joint where three members meet and two are collinear, the third is such a member. It may still brace the structure or carry load under different conditions, so zero does not mean useless.
card.after: In an ideal truss, a member can carry zero axial force under a particular load. At an unloaded joint with three members, if exactly two are collinear, the third is unloaded. It may still brace other members or carry force when the loading changes.

card.before: Control engineering makes systems follow desired behavior by using measured response to guide corrective action. A motor-speed controller, for example, compares a target with the actual speed and adjusts its output. Designing that feedback requires attention to how the system responds over time, not just its final setting.
card.after: Control engineering designs how systems follow desired behavior. In a feedback example, a motor-speed controller compares a target with measured speed and adjusts its output. Designing the controller requires attention to the response over time, including persistent error and overshoot.

card.before: A heat engine takes energy from a hot source, converts part into useful work, and rejects the rest to a cooler sink. A power plant’s steam can drive a generator while discarded heat goes to water or air. Both useful output and rejected heat belong in its energy accounting.
card.after: A cyclic heat engine takes energy from a hot source, converts part into useful work, and rejects the rest to a cooler sink. A power plant’s steam can drive a generator while discarded heat goes to water or air. Both outputs belong in its energy accounting.

card.before: PID control combines three responses to error: proportional action responds to the present error, integral action accumulates it, and derivative action responds to its rate of change. Adjusting their gains changes how a system approaches its target, including persistent offset, overshoot, and settling behavior.
card.after: In a basic formulation, PID control combines three responses to error: proportional action responds to present error, integral action accumulates it, and derivative action responds to its rate of change. Adjusting their gains changes how a system approaches its target, including persistent offset, overshoot, and settling.

card.before: Bumpless transfer switches between manual and automatic control without an abrupt jump in the commanded output. While manual control is active, the automatic controller tracks that signal and adjusts its internal state. When control changes hands, the outputs are already aligned rather than starting from unrelated values.
card.after: Bumpless transfer avoids an abrupt commanded-output jump when switching from manual to automatic control. One implementation lets the automatic controller track the manual signal and adjust its internal state before taking over, aligning the two outputs at the switching moment.

before.note: The source implements bumpless manual-to-automatic transfer using a PID controller’s tracking mode.

after.note: The cited MathWorks example uses a PID controller’s tracking mode to achieve manual-to-automatic bumpless transfer; this is an implementation example, not a claim that all bumpless transfer requires PID.

card.before: Cascade control nests a fast inner feedback loop inside a slower outer one. The outer controller sets the inner loop’s target, while the inner loop rejects local disturbances before they spread through the plant. The speed separation matters; simply stacking two controllers does not ensure this benefit.
card.after: Cascade control nests a fast inner feedback loop inside a slower outer one. The outer controller sets the inner loop’s target, while the inner loop helps reject local disturbances before they spread through the plant. Speed separation matters; stacking two controllers does not ensure this benefit.

card.before: The ideal rocket equation relates velocity change to effective exhaust speed and the logarithm of initial-to-final mass ratio. It assumes constant exhaust performance and neglects external losses such as gravity and drag. More propellant offers diminishing gains because that propellant initially adds to the mass being accelerated.
card.after: The ideal rocket equation links velocity change to constant effective exhaust speed and the logarithm of initial-to-final mass ratio, neglecting gravity and drag losses. At fixed dry mass, adding propellant gives diminishing velocity gains because the extra propellant must initially be accelerated too.

card.before: Pressure thrust is the nozzle-force contribution produced by a difference between exhaust pressure and surrounding pressure. It equals that difference multiplied by exit area and adds to the momentum-flow contribution. Matching the pressures removes this term, but does not remove the engine’s remaining thrust.
card.after: Pressure thrust is the force contribution from a difference between nozzle-exit and ambient pressure. With uniform exit pressure, it equals that difference times exit area, alongside momentum-flow thrust. Equal pressures remove this term, but need not remove the engine’s remaining thrust.

before.note: The source explicitly describes the variable-geometry converging-diverging nozzle used by afterburning engines.

after.note: NASA’s afterburning-engine example uses a variable-geometry converging-diverging nozzle; this is a supported design connection, not a claim that every variable-area nozzle has that form.

card.before: The Golden Gate Bridge’s 4,200-foot main span crossed a channel challenged by deep water, strong tides, and wind. It was the longest single span when completed. The project illustrates how bridge design must resolve site conditions and scale together, rather than treating span length as an isolated requirement.
card.after: The Golden Gate Bridge’s 4,200-foot main span was the world’s longest when built. Critics had called the channel too deep and its winds and tides too strong. The project illustrates how assessing a proposed crossing involves site conditions as well as span length.

card.before: Miter lock gates close as a pair forming a wide V across a chamber. In Panama’s original design, their hollow, watertight lower halves provide buoyancy that reduces hinge loading. A very large barrier can therefore retain water while requiring less support than its dry weight suggests.
card.after: Miter lock gates close as a pair forming a wide V across a chamber. In Panama’s original design, hollow, watertight lower halves provide buoyancy that reduces hinge loading. This reduces effective gate weight while the structure must still resist water-pressure forces.

card.before: A track circuit uses the rails as part of an electrical path to check whether a railway section is clear. A train shunts current away from a relay, changing the signal. This electrical indication lets the wider signalling system decide whether another train may safely proceed.
card.after: A track circuit uses the rails as part of an electrical path to detect whether a railway section is clear. In a basic relay-based arrangement, a train shunts current away from the relay. The wider signalling system uses this indication when deciding whether another train may proceed.

card.before: Track-circuit signalling often defaults to an occupied indication when a circuit fails. This can stop trains even when no train is actually present, because reliable clearance has been lost. The safer failure state trades uninterrupted service for protection against an uncertain section ahead.
card.after: Network Rail describes a fail-safe response in which a failed track circuit normally indicates occupancy. Trains can be stopped even when none is present because reliable clearance is lost. This favors a restrictive signal over uninterrupted service while the section’s status is uncertain.

card.before: Ramp metering uses traffic signals on entrance ramps to regulate how frequently vehicles enter a freeway. Releasing vehicles separately breaks up merging platoons that could force mainline traffic to brake. It can improve flow, but creates a ramp queue whose storage and effects must also be managed.
card.after: Ramp metering uses entrance-ramp signals to regulate freeway entry. Breaking up merging platoons can reduce sudden mainline braking and improve traffic flow. Metering also creates waiting queues, so its design must account for ramp storage and effects on adjacent streets.

card.before: In an ideal three-point bending test, a simply supported beam is loaded at its midpoint. Under linear-elastic, small-deflection beam theory, central deflection grows with load and span cubed, and decreases with elastic modulus and second moment of area. The model permits stiffness comparisons within those assumptions.
card.after: For a slender, uniform beam simply supported and loaded at its midpoint, an ideal three-point bending test links force and deflection. Linear-elastic, small-deflection beam theory predicts deflection proportional to load and span cubed, and inversely proportional to elastic modulus times second moment of area.
